title: American Indian outcomes require disaggregated measurement of place, history, governance, and identity
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35730, a methodological and historical essay on economic, educational, health, and human-capital heterogeneity among American Indians
geography: United States; American Indian populations and descendants of later arrivals, with urban-rural, tribal, resource, and historical-policy distinctions

observations.period: Paper issued September 2026; historical and contemporary measurement and policy context

denominator.unit: NBER methodological and historical essay; no single pooled population estimate

outcome_heterogeneity.unit: variation in economic, educational, and health outcomes across American Indian populations

structural_dimensions.unit: urban-rural location, resource endowments, tribal governance, and historical experiences with federal policy

historical_policy_persistence.unit: forced relocation, boarding schools, and assimilation policies on human-capital development and intergenerational mobility

self_governance_and_development.unit: recent outcomes where tribes exercise greater self-governance and implement economic-development strategies

measurement_boundary.unit: racial and tribal identification, changing definitions, and data limitations can obscure trends and policy effectiveness

observations.method: Methodological and historical synthesis of economic, educational, health, and human-capital evidence, emphasizing identification, tribal and racial classification, geography, historical policy, and governance heterogeneity.
observations.uncertainty: This paper is an essay and measurement critique rather than a single causal estimate or new pooled population survey. The abstract does not provide one common denominator, effect size, or policy evaluation across all American Indian populations; tribal identity, data coverage, and changing definitions limit direct comparison.
observations.subgroup: American Indian populations and descendants of later arrivals, differentiated by tribal affiliation, urban or rural location, resource endowments, historical exposure, self-governance, and economic-development strategy; these groups must not be pooled without an explicit estimand.
observations.counterinterpretation: Disaggregation can improve accuracy but may reduce comparability, sample size, privacy, and policy simplicity. Differences may reflect selection, geography, reporting, or institutional measurement as well as historical policy, and self-governance capacity is not uniform across tribes.

related_sources.claim: Official NBER DOI identifies the working paper.

boundary: This record establishes a measurement and governance boundary: American Indian outcomes are heterogeneous and historically conditioned, and data definitions can obscure both disparities and improvement. It does not provide a single causal estimate, rank tribes, establish current policy effectiveness, or substitute for tribal-specific evidence and sovereignty-aware interpretation.
